name: PiCCANTE
firmware_note: Single open-source firmware image with feature scaling by board: 2 CAN channels on a plain Pico/RP2040, 3 channels plus Wi-Fi/BLE config on a Pico 2 W/RP2350. No separate 'variant' firmware exists - it's one codebase.
price_note: No vendor sells this assembled. Parts-cost estimate for the minimal build: one Pico/RP2040 (~$4-5) plus one SN65HVD-class 3.3V CAN transceiver breakout (~$3-8). A 3-channel Pico 2 W build with three transceivers, wiring and a printed OBD-II shell runs closer to $30-45 in parts.
skill_note: You are sourcing parts, wiring or fabricating a PCB from the provided KiCAD files, removing stray 120-ohm termination resistors from generic transceiver breakouts, and flashing firmware yourself. Nothing is sold pre-built.
build_note: KiCAD PCB source and a 3D-printable OBD-II dongle shell are in the repo, but there is no assembled product or kit to buy from anyone. Minimal builds are perfboard and jumper wire.
summary: Open-source firmware that turns a Raspberry Pi Pico or Pico 2 (W) plus one to three 3.3V CAN transceivers into a multi-channel CAN bus sniffer and injector, speaking SLCAN/SocketCAN and SavvyCAN's GVRET protocol and partially emulating an ELM327 OBD-II adapter. It's a from-scratch, solder-it-yourself alternative to commercial CAN interfaces like CANtact or PCAN-USB.
honest_take: This is a hobbyist CAN interface, not a drop-in CANtact or Kvaser replacement: CAN FD and CAN XL are unsupported by design (the PIO-based bit-banging can't keep up with them), there's no hardware bus filtering yet, and the project's own docs call the ELM327 emulation partial - no adaptive timeouts, no auto protocol detection. There is also no vendor here at all: no assembled board, no warranty, no support contract, just a GitHub repo with 12 open issues. What the ~$15-45 in parts actually buys you is real multi-channel SocketCAN/SavvyCAN compatibility, which is the expensive part of commercial tools - budget your own time for the rest.
best_for: Learning CAN bus and automotive diagnostics for the cost of a Pico and a transceiver breakout
Multi-channel CAN capture on a near-zero budget per channel
SocketCAN or SavvyCAN workflows without buying a commercial dongle
not_for: CAN FD or CAN XL vehicles - unsupported by design
Turnkey use - there is no assembled product, you solder and flash this yourself
Heavy onboard logging - SD card support is still on the roadmap

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Dual-core Cortex-M0+ @133MHz on Pico/Pico W. A Pico 2/Pico 2 W (RP2350, dual Cortex-M33 or Hazard3 cores, up to 150MHz) is recommended for the full 3-channel build.

radios.note: Only present on Pico W/Pico 2 W builds, used for the optional web-based configuration interface and access point - not a wireless attack radio.

hardware.battery_note: USB-powered. The project advertises auto deep-sleep for always-connected OBD-II dongle use, not battery operation.
hardware.storage: None built in. SD card logging is listed as in-progress, not shipped.
connectivity: Wi-Fi (Pico W/2 W only, config only)
hardware.gpio: Standard Pico 40-pin GPIO; transceivers wired to PIO-driven pins
hardware.case: None included; a 3D-printable OBD-II dongle enclosure is provided as source files
notable_physical: KiCAD PCB design provided for anyone who wants to fab a proper board instead of perfboard

packet_capture.note: CAN 2.0B frame capture on up to 3 buses at once, exposed as SLCAN/SocketCAN interfaces and via SavvyCAN's GVRET binary protocol

scriptable.note: Open C/C++ firmware; the host side is driven by standard python-can / can-utils tooling over SocketCAN

web_ui.note: Only the Pico W / Pico 2 W builds run a web-based config page over their own Wi-Fi AP; the plain Pico has no Wi-Fi and no web UI at all

wifi_ap_mode.note: Config-only access point on Wi-Fi-capable boards, not a wireless attack feature

sd_logging.note: Listed as in-progress on the project roadmap; not implemented as of research date

standalone_untethered.note: A host running SavvyCAN, can-utils or a serial terminal is required; the Pico alone doesn't log or display captured traffic

i2c.note: Purpose-built CAN tool, not a general hardware-debug probe

logic_analyzer.note: The RP2040's PIO blocks are dedicated to CAN bit-timing, not exposed as a general-purpose analyzer

legal.notes: Reading CAN traffic on a vehicle you own for diagnostics is unremarkable almost everywhere. Injecting frames can disable safety-relevant systems while a vehicle is moving, and connecting to any vehicle, industrial machine or building system you don't own or have written authorization to test is a computer-misuse or property offence in most jurisdictions - the tool's low cost doesn't change that.

sources.what: feature list, supported transceivers, 2/3-channel split by board, GPL-3.0 license, 93 stars
KiCAD PCB source and confirmation no assembled kit is sold
ELM327 emulation caveats, SLCAN/GVRET protocol support, roadmap items (SD logging, MITM mode) marked unimplemented

research_gaps: No capability key exists for automotive CAN bus sniff/inject/ELM327-emulation as a category distinct from generic hardware-debug buses - the closest keys (uart/i2c/jtag_swd) don't fit and packet_capture is a stretch used here for CAN frames specifically
Exact release date / first-commit date not confirmed
No published current-draw or transceiver part recommendation beyond 'SN65HVD-class or similar 3.3V compatible'

name: PiKVM v4 Plus
firmware_note: The same open-source PiKVM OS used by every PiKVM reseller. Lab401 changes nothing about the software or hardware; it sells the stock V4 Plus under the name 'Hardware RAT' for the covert-implant market.
vendor: PiKVM (hardware); resold by Lab401 under a red-team-branded listing
price_note: EUR 359 direct from PiKVM's own store as of 2026-09-10 (~$420 converted at roughly 1.17 USD/EUR); a US reseller (Newegg) lists it around $540-568 with a discount applied. None of these prices include a cellular modem: the V4 Plus ships with an empty mPCIe slot and an empty nano-SIM slot, not a working modem. Yubico-class LTE/5G modules (Quectel EG25-G, SIMCom SIM7600G-H, Sierra Wireless MC7455) plus an antenna and SMA pigtail are separate purchases, typically $30-80 more.
skill_note: The device itself is plug-and-play once configured, but getting covert cellular connectivity working means sourcing and pairing a compatible LTE modem yourself, which the box does not include.
build_note: Fully assembled KVM-over-IP unit with metal case, pre-flashed microSD, ATX control board and cables. A cellular modem card, SIM and antenna must be bought and installed separately to use the LTE/5G slot at all.
summary: A Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 based KVM-over-IP unit: HDMI capture up to 1920x1200@60Hz, virtual keyboard/mouse/mass-storage emulation, Ethernet and Wi-Fi, plus an mPCIe slot and SIM slot for an LTE/5G modem so it can phone home over cellular instead of the target's network. It is PiKVM's own legitimate open-source sysadmin remote-management hardware; Lab401 resells the identical unit as a 'Hardware RAT' for red-team drop-in installs.
honest_take: Read PiKVM's own site and this is a sysadmin tool for managing datacenter servers - 'undetectable by antivirus' is Lab401's marketing language, not PiKVM's, and it's true only in the boring sense that a KVM dongle isn't malware running on the host OS, not in the sense that it's hard to notice physically. It genuinely is powerful for physical-access engagements: full keyboard/mouse/video/mass-storage control independent of the target's network. But the 'RAT' framing implies more covertness than you're buying - there's no modem in the box, the mPCIe and SIM slots are empty, and Lab401's page doesn't mention that. A real covert cellular install needs you to separately source a modem, SIM and antenna, adding cost, time and one more thing that can fail during an engagement.
best_for: Physical-access red-team engagements needing full KVM control independent of the target network
Legitimate remote datacenter/server management - its actual designed purpose
Situations where Ethernet/Wi-Fi access to the target network is undesirable or unavailable and you add your own cellular modem
not_for: Anyone expecting a modem in the box - it is not included
Fully covert installs without separately budgeting for a modem, SIM plan and antenna
Software-only engagements - this requires physical access to plug into the target's HDMI/USB

radios.note: CM4's onboard 2.4/5GHz Wi-Fi; used for network management, not scanning/attack
mPCIe slot with USB lines plus a nano-SIM slot for a user-supplied LTE/5G modem; no modem ships in the box

hardware.battery_note: Mains powered via 12V barrel/DC input; no internal battery
notable_physical: ATX control board with cables and brackets for host power management

hdmi_capture.note: Up to 1920x1200@60Hz with audio, via the HDMI-in port

usb_hid_inject.note: Emulates a USB keyboard and mouse to the target host - this is the KVM's core control mechanism, not a BadUSB-style payload injector

usb_mass_storage.note: Emulates a virtual CD-ROM/flash drive and can mount remote disk images to the target

cloud_c2.note: PiKVM Cloud and remote-access features let it be reached over the internet, including via the optional cellular modem; not independently tested for this record

ethernet_mitm.note: It is a KVM peripheral emulator, not an inline network tap or MITM device

usb_keylogger.note: Commonly assumed because it sits 'between' keyboard and host in some setups, but PiKVM emulates a peripheral to the target - it does not log the target's own outbound keystrokes

standalone_untethered.note: Runs headless once configured; needs mains power but no attached laptop

scriptable.note: REST API and Arch Linux ARM userland with package manager access

wifi_ap_mode.note: PiKVM documents first-boot Wi-Fi client configuration via SD-card files; whether it can also run as its own AP for setup was not confirmed

legal.notes: Connecting this to a machine or network you don't own or have explicit written authorization to access is a computer-misuse offence in most jurisdictions, independent of how the hardware is marketed. Cellular connectivity via an installed modem also means the operator's SIM/carrier account is directly traceable to the install.

name: Multipick Kronos EPG
firmware: n/a - motorized mechanical tool, no firmware
vendor: Multipick (sold in the security-tool market as 'Kronos Electric Pick' by Lab401 and others)
price_note: EUR 215 at Lab401 (~$232 converted at roughly 1.08 USD/EUR on 2026-09-10). Multipick's own US store lists the same base unit at $250.52, and a 'Kronos Complete Electric Lock Pick Set' bundle with a hard case and extra needles at $483.56. Prices vary further by regional reseller (KeyPrint UK, LockPickWorld US, etc.).
skill_note: Consistent tension and needle placement matter more than raw power; reviewers describe real competence as taking deliberate practice, more so on security-pin cylinders.
build_note: Ships ready to use: gun body, 5 replacement 0.5mm pick needles, 2 tension wrenches, Allen key for needle swaps, USB charge cable.
summary: A German-made (Multipick) motorized electric pick gun for non-destructive opening of pin-tumbler profile cylinders, including many standard high-security cylinders. A DC motor drives a needle at up to 13,000 strokes/minute with adjustable 1-4mm stroke amplitude, aimed at locksmiths and physical-penetration testers rather than hobbyists.
honest_take: This is a pin-tumbler tool and only a pin-tumbler tool: it is explicitly not effective on disc-detainer, dimple or wafer locks, which is the most common misconception buyers have about 'electric pick guns' in general - people assume one tool defeats all lock families the way a Flipper is assumed to defeat all RFID. Vendor claims of opening '75%+ of locks with practice' are for standard pin-tumbler cylinders under favorable conditions; tight keyways and genuine security pins still demand real skill and time, motor or no motor. At $232-250 for the bare unit it undercuts hand-picking training time, but it is not a shortcut past lock-picking skill - it automates the raking motion, not the reading of pins.
best_for: Physical penetration testers who already understand pin-tumbler picking and want speed on standard/euro-profile cylinders
Locksmiths doing high-volume non-destructive entry on ordinary pin-tumbler stock
Quiet operation - reviewers consistently note it as one of the quietest electric picks available
not_for: Disc-detainer, dimple or wafer locks - not what this tool is built for
Beginners expecting the motor to substitute for picking skill
High-security cylinders without prior manual picking experience - the motor doesn't read pins for you

hardware.mcu_primary_note: No microcontroller; a DC motor and mechanical stroke mechanism, not an electronic/firmware device
hardware.battery_note: 3.7V/2900mAh Li-Ion, approx. 2.5 hours continuous runtime, USB charging
hardware.case: Handheld gun body; hard-shell carrying case included only with the 'Complete Set' bundle
notable_physical: Adjustable 1-4mm stroke amplitude at the needle chuck
Interchangeable 0.5mm pick needles via Allen key

standalone_untethered.note: Battery powered, no host device or software needed to operate

hid_remote_trigger.note: Trigger is a manual switch on the gun body; no wireless/remote actuation

scriptable.note: Purely mechanical/electromechanical tool, no programmable logic

hf_1356_read.note: Purely mechanical pick, no RFID/NFC capability despite sharing shelf space with electronic access-control tools

legal.notes: Possession of lock-picking tools is legal in most US states and much of Europe for personal or professional use, but a handful of US states and other countries restrict possession without a locksmith license or 'burglary tool' intent, and using it on a lock you don't own or lack authorization to open is a property/burglary offence everywhere. Check your local law before buying or carrying it.

sources.what: EUR 215 price, included accessories, 13,000 RPM and 1-4mm stroke claims, battery spec
official manufacturer price ($250.52), Complete Set bundle price ($483.56), dimensions, weight, runtime
independent review (BosnianBill's LockLab) confirming pin-tumbler focus and not being suited to disc-detainer/dimple/wafer locks
independent locksmith trade review corroborating quiet operation and skill-dependent success rate

A dedicated 'physical-access' category and picking-specific capability keys (e.g. pin_tumbler_pick, high_security_pick) would fit this device and similar tools far better

name: LilyGo T-Deck Plus
firmware: Meshtastic / MeshCore (community firmware; ships without a security-focused firmware)
firmware_note: LilyGo ships the board as a bare development platform - you flash Meshtastic, MeshCore or your own ESP-IDF/Arduino code. No offensive-security firmware ships by default, unlike the Bruce-flashed LilyGo boards elsewhere in this database.
price_note: $85 at Hacker Warehouse for the Plus kit (board, LoRa module, GPS, 2000mAh battery, antenna, case). LILYGO's own store and other resellers list the same kit in a similar $80-90 band depending on the LoRa frequency SKU (868/915/923 MHz).
skill_note: Arrives as a development platform, not a finished security tool - you choose and flash firmware yourself, and Meshtastic/MeshCore setup assumes some comfort with ESP32 flashing tools.
build_note: Fully assembled handheld (keyboard, screen, GPS, battery, case). No soldering; flashing firmware via USB is the only setup step.
summary: A BlackBerry-style ESP32-S3 handheld with a QWERTY keyboard, trackball, 2.8-inch IPS touchscreen, SX1262 LoRa radio, GPS and a 2000mAh battery, sold as a Meshtastic/MeshCore off-grid mesh communicator. It is a general-purpose ESP32-S3 dev platform that happens to carry LoRa and GPS, not a purpose-built security tool.
honest_take: Like other LoRa/GPS handhelds in this space, people see 'LoRa + GPS + keyboard' and assume it's a Flipper-class attack tool; it isn't one out of the box. There is no sub-GHz CC1101, no NFC/RFID reader, and no offensive firmware pre-loaded - the SX1262 is a LoRa/FSK part locked to whichever frequency SKU you bought, not a general sub-GHz scanner, and Meshtastic itself has no attack tooling at all. What you're buying for $85 is a capable ESP32-S3 dev board with a keyboard and screen already built - a good base if you intend to write or port your own BLE/Wi-Fi tooling, a poor buy if you expected a mesh-networking Flipper.
best_for: Meshtastic/MeshCore off-grid text messaging - its designed purpose
A keyboard-and-screen-equipped ESP32-S3 platform for your own firmware projects
GPS-tagged field logging
not_for: Sub-GHz replay/brute-force attacks - no CC1101-class radio
RFID/NFC work - no reader hardware
Anyone expecting pre-loaded offensive Wi-Fi/BLE tooling - it ships as a bare dev platform

radios.note: LoRa/(G)FSK transceiver, band fixed by SKU (868/915/923MHz depending on region variant); not a general-purpose 300-928MHz scanner
ESP32-S3 integrated 2.4GHz Wi-Fi 4 and BLE 5; no 5GHz, no Bluetooth Classic
Branded 'Ulbox GPS' by resellers; exact chip not published by LILYGO

name: Glytch GPS Mod for Pager
firmware: n/a - passive GNSS module read by the Pager's own gpsd service
firmware_note: No firmware of its own. The WiFi Pineapple Pager's existing gpsd-based GPS support reads it once you set Settings > GPS to the correct serial device and baud rate.
price_note: $60 direct from Hak5. Seen at EUR 79 (~$85) at Lab401 and around $85.32 at other regional resellers (e.g. KSEC) - roughly 40% over Hak5's own price once converted.
skill_note: Plugs into the Pager's USB port; the only setup step is picking the right serial device and baud rate in the Pager's Settings > GPS menu.
build_note: Hand-assembled, 3D-printed enclosure that clips on and connects over USB - no soldering. Vendor notes it 'may show variations typical of handcrafted hardware.'
summary: A small 3D-printed, hand-assembled add-on carrying a Quectel LC86-series multi-constellation GNSS chipset, connecting to the WiFi Pineapple Pager over USB to geotag its Wi-Fi survey and attack logs via the Pager's built-in gpsd support. It requires a WiFi Pineapple Pager as the host - it has no function on its own.
honest_take: This is exactly what it says: a GPS receiver in a box, nothing more. It adds Wigle-compatible geotagging to wardriving logs the Pager already collects - it does not add any new attack capability. Accuracy is ordinary consumer GNSS (a few meters outdoors with clear sky, degraded or absent indoors), fine for venue-scale wardriving, not for anything needing tight geofence precision. It's a genuinely single-purpose accessory, so don't expect much beyond 'the Pager now knows where it is' - and remember it does nothing without a Pager to plug into.

Wigle-compatible wardriving with the Pager
Venue-scale signal mapping
not_for: Any use without owning a WiFi Pineapple Pager - this has no standalone function
High-accuracy geofencing - consumer GNSS accuracy only
Indoor positioning - GNSS degrades or fails indoors like any consumer GPS

name: YubiKey NEO
price_note: $50 last listed at Hacker Warehouse, now out of stock. Yubico discontinued the NEO around 2018 in favor of the YubiKey 4/5 lines; remaining stock is old inventory or secondhand.
skill_note: Plug-and-play OTP out of the box; configuring PIV/OpenPGP smart-card slots needs Yubico's management tools.
summary: A discontinued (2012-2018) dual-interface USB+NFC hardware authentication token supporting Yubico OTP, OATH (TOTP/HOTP), FIDO U2F, and PIV/OpenPGP smart-card functions. It is an authentication device, not an offensive or defensive pentest tool, included here because vendors like Hacker Warehouse stock it as a cheap way to demonstrate hardware-backed authentication.
honest_take: The single biggest thing to know: the NEO predates FIDO2/WebAuthn entirely and cannot do it - it only speaks the older FIDO U2F protocol. In 2026, passkeys and FIDO2 are what most 'phishing-resistant auth' deployments actually mean, and this device cannot fill that role no matter how it's marketed. It's a fine, cheap way to demonstrate that hardware OTP/U2F exists and what it feels like to tap a key, but if the goal is to show or use modern passkey-based authentication, a current YubiKey 5-series (or similar FIDO2 token) is the correct purchase, not this discontinued unit. It was not affected by the 2017 ROCA RSA-key-generation flaw that hit YubiKey 4 - that's one thing it has going for it.
best_for: Cheap demonstration of legacy OTP/U2F hardware authentication in a training or awareness context
PIV/OpenPGP smart-card use on systems that don't need FIDO2
not_for: Demonstrating or deploying modern passkey/FIDO2/WebAuthn authentication - it does not support the protocol at all
Any production security deployment in 2026 - Yubico stopped selling and supporting it years ago
Anyone who actually wants FIDO2 - buy a current YubiKey 5-series instead

standalone_untethered.note: Needs a host USB port or NFC reader to do anything

legal.notes: An authentication device with no offensive capability; owning and using it is unremarkable everywhere. The only legal consideration is organizational - using outdated auth hardware that can't do FIDO2 may fail compliance requirements that specify passkey/WebAuthn support.

summary: A 12-LED high-intensity infrared blaster board for the Flipper Zero GPIO header, designed for a tight, long-throw beam so you can hit a device across a room without aiming precisely. It's Rabbit-Labs' mid/high-power tier, sitting between their cheaper 7-LED 'Original IR Blaster' and their wide-angle-flood 'Slim Shady' board.
honest_take: Same story as every powered IR add-on in this niche: it is a resistor-and-LED array, not a chip - the $50 buys Rabbit-Labs' thermal design and focused-beam optics, not silicon. It also needs GPIO 5V mode enabled and, per the vendor's own listing, unofficial firmware with Debug IR turned on, which the cheaper 7-LED 'Original IR Blaster' explicitly does not require ('works out-of-the-box with official firmware'). If you don't want to touch GPIO settings or flash unofficial firmware, the cheaper board is the easier buy; if you specifically want a tight, long-range 'throw' beam rather than wide flood coverage, this is the one in the Rabbit-Labs lineup built for that.

summary: A GPIO shield plus companion Flipper Zero app that adds RS485 differential signaling and voltage-level shifting, letting the Flipper sniff and inject Modbus RTU traffic on industrial control networks - PLCs, sensors, actuators and similar serial-bus ICS/OT equipment.
honest_take: This is a rare, genuinely niche addition to the Flipper ecosystem: real ICS/OT protocol testing (sniff Modbus RTU frames, build and send requests by peripheral ID/function code/address, replay captured packets) rather than another RFID or sub-GHz board. The vendor is upfront that Modbus RTU has no built-in authentication or encryption - which is the industrial-protocol reality, not a flaw in this tool - so anything you can address on the bus you can generally write to. It's explicitly billed as 'designed and built for authorized security testing'; there's no ambiguity about what it's for.

Learning industrial protocol structure hands-on with real hardware
Sniffing and replaying Modbus traffic for lab/test-bench work

name: ChimeraBLE
firmware_note: Firmware only. Three build targets share one BLE engine: generic ESP32 WROOM (serial CLI), Seeed XIAO ESP32-C5 (serial CLI), and M5Stack Cardputer ADV (onboard graphical UI).
price_note: No vendor product for the ESP32/XIAO-C5 targets (~$5-10 generic board). The Cardputer ADV target requires M5Stack's ~$40-50 Cardputer ADV hardware, sold separately by M5Stack.

build_note: Flash onto generic ESP32/XIAO ESP32-C5, or onto an M5Stack Cardputer ADV for the graphical-UI build. No soldering for any target.
summary: Open-source BLE security and reverse-engineering firmware for ESP32 that can act as a scanning/enumerating central, a cloned/emulated peripheral, or both simultaneously as a man-in-the-middle proxy. It does full GATT service/characteristic/descriptor enumeration with SIG UUID resolution, decodes HID report maps to show live keystrokes from a connected keyboard, clones a device's GATT tree with MAC spoofing, and includes RSSI-based direction finding ('fox-hunting').
honest_take: The 'MITM' capability here is impersonation-based, not over-the-air interception: ChimeraBLE connects to the real device as a central and simultaneously advertises a cloned peripheral to the victim host, proxying traffic between the two active connections it holds. That is a real and useful attack, but it is not the same thing as passively following an existing BLE connection's frequency-hopping pattern the way a dedicated sniffer (Ubertooth, Sniffle-class nRF52 dongle) does - ChimeraBLE cannot eavesdrop on a connection it isn't a party to. Cloned characteristics also run without encryption and can't replicate bonding-protected access, so a device relying on BLE bonding for security will not be fully fooled by the clone. It's a genuinely capable, actively developed multi-role tool for the price of a $5-10 board - just don't expect passive network-level sniffing.

not_for: Passive, promiscuous BLE sniffing of a connection you're not part of - it has no radio/firmware capability for following connection hopping
Cloning devices that rely on BLE bonding/pairing security - clones run unencrypted and can't replicate bonded access

firmware_note: Firmware only, targets a generic ESP32-WROOM-32 dev board. Uses the third-party ESP32 BLE Keyboard library (T-vK).
price_note: No vendor product; a generic ESP32-WROOM-32 dev board costs roughly $5-10.

summary: Open-source firmware that turns an ESP32 into a BLE HID keyboard emulator, running Ducky Script-style keystroke payloads (open apps, type URLs, run commands) once paired with a target across Windows, macOS, Linux and Android. Positioned as a wireless alternative to a USB Rubber Ducky that doesn't need physical USB port access.
honest_take: The 'no physical USB access needed' pitch is real but comes with a big asterisk the project name doesn't advertise: unlike a USB Rubber Ducky, which a target device trusts instantly on physical insertion, this requires the victim to see and accept a Bluetooth pairing prompt the first time - it is not silent on first contact. After that initial pairing it can auto-reconnect quietly, so the realistic attack path is 'get physical access once to pair it, walk away, trigger payloads remotely later,' not 'wave it near an unlocked laptop and go.' It only works against hosts that accept unauthenticated BLE HID pairing, which is common but not universal. At 42 GitHub stars this is a small, lightly-used project compared to established BadUSB tooling - expect rougher edges.

name: OsmocomBB
firmware_note: Open Layer 1/2/3 GSM baseband firmware for TI Calypso-chipset phones, replacing the phone's proprietary baseband software entirely.
price_note: No vendor product - you buy a used Calypso-chipset feature phone (Motorola C118/C121/C123/C139/C140/C155/V171, historically $2-3 each, more realistically $5-20 on eBay in 2026) and flash it with this open firmware. A cheap serial/USB cable to the phone is usually needed too.
skill_note: Requires understanding GSM's Layer 1/2/3 stack, sourcing a discontinued phone model on the secondhand market, and running the host-side layer23 applications yourself - there is no beginner path here.
build_note: No kit exists. You source a specific secondhand Calypso-chipset Motorola/Sony Ericsson phone, flash OsmocomBB's firmware onto it, and run the PC-side layer2/3 applications (mobile, ccch_scan, cell_log) over a cable link to the phone.
summary: Open-source GSM baseband firmware for old TI Calypso-chipset feature phones (Motorola C1xx/C139/C155/V171 family), giving full open access to the GSM Layer 1/2/3 stack for protocol research: scanning control channels, logging cell info, and - because 2G's A5/1 encryption and lack of mutual network authentication are both weak - passive research into IMSI-catching and control-channel interception on 2G networks specifically. It is GSM (2G) only; it has no 3G/4G/5G capability of any kind, because those protocols don't run on this hardware or firmware at all.
honest_take: Be blunt about what this still gets you in 2026: it is 2G-only, full stop, and 2G is actively being shut down worldwide. US carriers finished their 2G sunsets years ago; multiple European and Asian operators (France's Orange, the Netherlands, Japan, several in Vietnam and Thailand) have 2026 shutdown dates; roughly 70 countries have 2G phase-outs completed or scheduled. That doesn't make OsmocomBB useless - a substantial minority of countries (Saudi Arabia explicitly says it will run 2G indefinitely, and 21 countries have no published shutdown plan at all) still carry live 2G traffic, and it remains the standard open-source reference for GSM air-interface research and teaching regardless of live-network availability. But if the goal is real-world interception capability against a modern phone in a market that has sunset 2G, this tool cannot reach it - the target phone will simply refuse to fall back to a network this hardware can speak to. And this is entirely a research/education tool with a discontinued hardware dependency: you're hunting 15-20-year-old phones on eBay, not buying anything current.
best_for: GSM (2G) protocol research and education in jurisdictions/labs where 2G is still live or in a controlled test network
Understanding 2G's real security weaknesses (weak A5/1, no mutual authentication) hands-on
Layer 1/2/3 GSM stack development and experimentation
not_for: Any interception or research targeting 3G, 4G or 5G networks - architecturally impossible with this hardware/firmware
Use in any country/carrier that has completed its 2G sunset - there is no 2G signal to interact with
Turnkey or beginner use - sourcing discontinued phones and running the host-side toolchain both require real GSM protocol knowledge

hardware.mcu_primary_note: GSM baseband chipset used in Motorola C11x/C12x/C139/C140/C155/V171-family phones from the mid-2000s; OsmocomBB replaces the phone's stock baseband firmware entirely

radios.note: GSM 2G only (850/900/1800/1900MHz band-dependent on phone model). No 3G/4G/5G capability - those protocols require entirely different silicon this hardware does not have.

hardware.battery_note: Original phone battery, typically old/degraded on secondhand units
connectivity: Serial/USB cable link to host PC for layer2/3 applications
hardware.case: Original phone chassis (Motorola C1xx-family candybar form factor)
notable_physical: Standard feature-phone keypad and small LCD from the donor handset

sdr_rx.note: Not an SDR - this is real GSM baseband silicon (TI Calypso) confined to standard GSM channels/bands, not a wideband tunable receiver like an SDR

sdr_tx.note: Same reasoning: fixed-function GSM baseband, not general-purpose RF transmit

packet_capture.note: The ccch_scan/layer23 host tooling can dump received GSM Layer 1 frames and forward them as GSMTAP packets to Wireshark for analysis

scriptable.note: Open C source for both firmware and host-side layer2/3 applications (mobile, cell_log, ccch_scan)

standalone_untethered.note: Layer 1 runs on the phone; Layer 2/3 processing happens on a host PC connected over a serial/USB link - the phone alone cannot do protocol research work

jtag_swd.note: Some Calypso hardware hacking exists in the broader community, but it isn't a stated focus or documented feature of the OsmocomBB project itself

legal.notes: GSM interception and IMSI-catching are tightly regulated or outright illegal for non-licensed operators in most countries, regardless of how cheap or old the hardware is - many jurisdictions treat any unauthorized reception/decoding of mobile network control-channel data, and certainly any active network impersonation, as a serious telecommunications-interception offence carrying criminal penalties. Passive academic research on your own isolated test network (e.g. via OpenBTS/osmocom-bts in a Faraday-shielded lab) is a very different legal position from anything touching live commercial spectrum or real subscriber traffic - treat the two as entirely separate activities and check local telecom law before doing either.

sources.what: 331 stars, project description as a Mobile Station-side GSM implementation for Calypso-chipset phones
ccch_scan tool: dumps received GSM Layer 1 frames, forwards as GSMTAP to Wireshark, used for control-channel research
Motorola C123/C121/C118 setup guide confirming supported phone models and the E88 firmware variant used

2026 country-by-country 2G/3G sunset timeline: 19+ countries completed, ~70 countries/139 operators with plans, France/Netherlands/Japan/Vietnam/Thailand 2026 shutdown dates, Saudi Arabia's indefinite-2G stance, 21 countries with no published plan

explains why 2G specifically is vulnerable (weak A5/1 cipher, no mutual authentication) and that OsmocomBB-based research targets exactly this weakness - marked as community-sourced, not primary/official documentation

research_gaps: No capability key exists for cellular/GSM functions at all (passive IMSI catching, control-channel sniffing, cell scanning) - sdr_rx/tx are used here only to explicitly rule out SDR framing, not to describe what the device actually does; a dedicated cellular category and keys (e.g. gsm_2g_only, imsi_catch_passive, cell_scan) are needed for this and any future cellular tool in the database

Whether any currently-manufactured phone still uses a Calypso-compatible chipset was not found - this appears to depend entirely on 15-20-year-old discontinued secondhand hardware, which is itself a supply-risk finding worth flagging
Precise list of which of the ~70 countries with 2G phase-out plans have already gone dark versus still pending as of September 2026 was not itemized country-by-country
